title: Reconstruction and rigidity for schemes from locally ringed etale topoi
statement: Work in the universes of [def-weil-size-convention]. Let $U,V$ be schemes [def-pc-scheme] with small etale sites [def-weil-pbc-etale-site] and structure sheaves $\mathcal O_U(T)=\Gamma(T,\mathcal O_T)$. Use ringed-topos morphisms [def-weil-pbc-ringed-topos-morphism]. A locally ringed topos here means a ringed topos whose ring sheaf has locally $a$ or $1-a$ invertible for every section $a$, and whose equalizer of $0,1$ is the initial sheaf. A local morphism means that its square of ring sheaves and unit subsheaves is cartesian. These etale ringed topoi are locally ringed, and every scheme morphism $a:U\to V$ induces a local ringed-topos morphism $(a_{\mathrm{et}},a^\sharp)$. For every local ringed-topos morphism $g:(\operatorname{Sh}(U_{\mathrm{et}}),\mathcal O_U)\to(\operatorname{Sh}(V_{\mathrm{et}}),\mathcal O_V)$ there is a unique scheme morphism $a:U\to V$ whose induced ringed-topos morphism is isomorphic to $g$. An isomorphism means a natural isomorphism of inverse-image functors commuting with the structural ring maps. Every ring-compatible natural endomorphism of $a_{\mathrm{et}}^{-1}$ is the identity. In particular any two isomorphisms from $g$ to the morphism induced by $a$ coincide. There are no separation, quasi-compactness or finite-type hypotheses.

proof.text: First verify that the stated local-ringedness holds. For a section $s\in\Gamma(T,\mathcal O_T)$ on an etale object $T\to U$, the principal opens $D(s)$ and $D(1-s)$ cover $T$: in each local ring at least one of $s,1-s$ is a unit. On these two opens respectively $s$ and $1-s$ is invertible. If $0=1$ on $T$, then every local ring of $T$ is zero, so $T$ is empty. Conversely the empty scheme has its unique section. Thus the equalizer of $0,1$ is the initial sheaf, including when $U$ is empty.

source.place: Tag 04HZ (lemma-etale-site-locally-ringed); direct sectionwise verification of its two conditions.

proof.text: For a scheme morphism $a:U\to V$, the cited algebraic inverse-image statement supplies the geometric adjunction on sets and its induced ring objects. Pullback of functions on $T\to V$ to $U\times_VT$ gives $\mathcal O_V\to a_*\mathcal O_U$; its adjunct is $a^\sharp$. It preserves the ring operations because pullback of functions does. On a geometric stalk $\bar u$, the germ formula identifies its map with the local map of strict local rings attached to $a$ by strict-henselization functoriality: both send a function on a pointed etale neighbourhood to its pullback. To check the unit square, form the map from $a^{-1}\mathcal O_V^\times$ to the fibre product of $a^{-1}\mathcal O_V$ with $\mathcal O_U^\times$. On each geometric stalk it is bijective, since a local ring homomorphism reflects units. Stalks commute with the finite products and equalizers defining units and this fibre product. The cited stalk detection makes that comparison an isomorphism; hence the square is cartesian. The same pullback formula identifies composites and identities.

Prove faithfulness before reconstructing anything. Suppose a ring-compatible isomorphism $t:a^{-1}\cong b^{-1}$ is given for scheme maps $a,b:U\to V$. On an open $H\subset V$, the representable pullback formula identifies their images of $h_H$ with $h_{a^{-1}H}$ and $h_{b^{-1}H}$. These are subobjects of the terminal object; naturality at $h_H\to1$ implies that their subobjects coincide. Thus $a^{-1}H=b^{-1}H$ for every open $H$. Scheme points are distinguished by opens: if two points lie in a common affine open they are prime ideals distinguished by a principal open, and if they do not lie in a common affine open, an affine neighbourhood of one already distinguishes them. Therefore $a,b$ have the same underlying map. A section $s\in\mathcal O_V(H)$ is the sheaf map $h_H\to\mathcal O_V$ given by pullback of $s$. Naturality of $t$ for this map, followed by ring compatibility, gives $a^\sharp(s)=b^\sharp(s)$ on the common inverse open. Hence the maps of structure sheaves agree and $a=b$ as scheme morphisms.

Next prove rigidity. For a ring-compatible natural endomorphism $t$ of $a^{-1}$ and an affine etale $T\to V$, choose the coordinates and monomorphism $e_a$ supplied by the cited coordinate lemma. Naturality with the coordinate map, and $a^\sharp t_{\mathcal O_V}=a^\sharp$, give $e_a t_{h_T}=e_a$, using that $a^{-1}$ preserves finite products. Since $e_a$ is monic, $t_{h_T}=1$. Take a small affine cover-dense set of etale objects using the cited smallness statement. Every sheaf has a coequalizer presentation by coproducts of these representables; they are already sheaves by subcanonicity. The inverse image is a left adjoint, so it preserves these small colimits. Naturality with the coproduct inclusions and the coequalizer map now forces $t_F=1$ for every sheaf $F$: first its components on the coproducts are identity, and then equality follows after the coequalizer map. This proves the endomorphism assertion for arbitrary $U,V$.

Let now $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$, $V=\operatorname{Spec}B$ and $g$ be local. Form $\varphi:B\to A$ on global sections and $a=\operatorname{Spec}\varphi$. The affine-solution comparison gives natural isomorphisms $g^{-1}h_T\cong h_{U\times_VT}$ on affine etale $T\to V$. For any sheaf $F$ on $U_{\mathrm{et}}$, evaluation and adjunction give
$$(g_*F)(T)=\operatorname{Hom}(h_T,g_*F)=\operatorname{Hom}(g^{-1}h_T,F)\cong F(U\times_VT)=(a_*F)(T).$$
The evaluation bijection sends a map from $h_T$ to the image of $\mathrm{id}_T$; its inverse pulls that section back along each arrow to $T$. Thus it is natural in both variables. Affine-site restriction is an equivalence, so these isomorphisms extend uniquely to a natural isomorphism $g_*\cong a_*$. The adjunction bijections then give an isomorphism of their left adjoints. It respects the structural ring maps: on an affine etale $T=\operatorname{Spec}C$, its equality on every $c\in C$ is exactly the evaluation identity in the affine-solution comparison; these affine values determine a sheaf map by the same restriction equivalence. Consequently $g$ is ring-isomorphic to the morphism induced by $a$. Step 3 gives uniqueness of $a$, and step 4 gives uniqueness of the isomorphism, by composing one isomorphism with the inverse of the other.

Record how restrictions will be used. The localization equivalence identifies sheaves on the site $U_{\mathrm{et}}/W$ with the topos slice over $h_W$. For an open subscheme $W\subset U$, the cited etale-site localization identifies this site with $W_{\mathrm{et}}$: an etale scheme over $U$ factoring through $W$ is precisely an etale scheme over $W$, with the same arrows and covering families. The structure rings coincide objectwise, both being $T\mapsto\Gamma(T,\mathcal O_T)$. Thus these are identifications of ringed topoi. The cited ringed-slice functoriality restricts $g$ to these slices, keeps locality, and identifies successive restrictions and restrictions of ring-compatible isomorphisms. Composition with an open inclusion is the same restriction on the source. Indeed its inverse image on an etale object over the open is ordinary restriction, and its ring map is pullback of functions. Composition stays local: its unit square is the paste of the two cartesian unit squares, since inverse images preserve finite limits.

proof.text: Suppose $V$ is affine and $U$ arbitrary. Choose a small affine open cover $U=\bigcup_iU_i$. Apply step 5 to $g$ restricted to each $U_i$, using step 6, obtaining $a_i:U_i\to V$ and ring-compatible isomorphisms to the restricted $g$. On $U_i\cap U_j$, both restricted induced morphisms are ring-isomorphic to the same restriction of $g$. Step 3, which has no affineness hypothesis, gives equality of the scheme maps on this overlap. The cited scheme-morphism gluing produces $a:U\to V$. Step 4 shows that the isomorphisms on $U_i\cap U_j$ agree: their ratio is an automorphism of the induced morphism there. Glue their components explicitly: for a sheaf $F$ on $V_{\mathrm{et}}$ and etale $T\to U$, use the open cover $T\times_UU_i$ of $T$. The local images of each section agree on double overlaps and hence give a unique section of $g^{-1}F(T)$. Gluing the inverses in the same way gives a bijection. Restriction maps, naturality in $F$ and ring compatibility hold locally and therefore globally by uniqueness in the sheaf axiom. This is the required ring-compatible isomorphism for affine $V$ and arbitrary $U$.

source.place: Tag 04I7 (theorem-fully-faithful), first existence paragraph and the following 2-isomorphism gluing diagram.

proof.text: For arbitrary $V$, choose a small affine open cover $V=\bigcup_\lambda V_\lambda$. Finite-limit preservation makes $g^{-1}h_{V_\lambda}$ subterminal, so the cited subterminal classification writes it uniquely as $h_{W_\lambda}$ for an open $W_\lambda\subset U$. These opens cover $U$. Indeed $1$ is the coequalizer of the two arrows from the coproduct of the pairwise intersections of the $h_{V_\lambda}$ to their coproduct: sections glue uniquely on the open covering, which proves this coequalizer property directly. The left adjoint $g^{-1}$ preserves these small colimits and finite intersections; thus the analogous coproduct of the $h_{W_\lambda}$ maps epimorphically to $1$. If their union were a proper open, this epimorphism would factor through the proper subterminal $h_{\bigcup W_\lambda}\hookrightarrow1$, which must itself be an epimorphism since the composite is one. The cited mono-epi criterion makes this subterminal inclusion an isomorphism. Evaluating at the terminal etale object then says that $U$ factors through $\bigcup W_\lambda$. Hence their union is $U$. Steps 6 and 7 give a map $a_\lambda:W_\lambda\to V_\lambda$ and a ring-isomorphism with the localized $g$.

source.place: Tag 04I7 (theorem-fully-faithful), final paragraph, construction of W and localized g.

proof.text: Regard $a_\lambda$ as maps $W_\lambda\to V$. On $W_\lambda\cap W_\mu$ their induced ringed morphisms are both isomorphic to the restriction of $g$ (step 6). Faithfulness (step 3) gives equality of these maps. Scheme gluing gives $a:U\to V$. Rigidity (step 4) makes the ring-compatible isomorphisms agree on every overlap, so the componentwise sheaf gluing of step 7 produces $a_{\mathrm{et}}^{-1}\cong g^{-1}$ with compatible structure maps. This proves existence globally. If $b$ is another reconstructed map, compose its isomorphism with the inverse of the one for $a$ and apply step 3 to obtain $a=b$. If two isomorphisms from $g$ to the induced morphism are given, compose one with the inverse of the other to get an endomorphism of $a_{\mathrm{et}}^{-1}$; step 4 makes it the identity, so the isomorphisms coincide. No step required affine overlaps or a finite cover.
